items.title: A beginner’s guide to falling in love with Russian literature
items.description:
Few literary canons inspire as much reverence, and fear, as Russia’s. The sheer size and complexity of novels like Leo Tolstoy’s  War and Peace  (1867) and Fyodor Dostoevsky’s  The Brothers Karamazov  (1880) have created two groups of readers: Those who have read them, and those who say they will read them — one day.

items.title: The body keeps exposing how much we don’t understand
items.description:
“We have so much opportunity still and so much room to grow. Science is never done.” 
 Inside the Nike Sport Research Lab, Chief Science Officer Matthew Nurse and his team chase the questions that hold athletes back. Drawing on biomechanics, physiology and neuroscience, they start with the problems every athlete knows: fatigue, injury, the moment the body gives out. items.title: A “theory” has a special meaning in science
items.description: Whenever someone tells you that they “have a theory,” you’re probably a mix of curious and skeptical, and with good reason. items.title: Why political fights devolve into wars about words
items.description:
In August 2024, I moved with my family from Chicago, Illinois, to Milan, Italy, to test out living overseas for a year. items.title: You’re allowed to be happy. In fact, you have a duty to be.
items.description:
Albert Camus and Simone de Beauvoir were having a drink when de Beauvoir asked how anybody can be happy in a world so full of misery. How can they laugh and drink and dance when millions of people are being murdered and abused?

items.title: Scholars still can’t define religion. Here’s why
items.description: Scholars of religion still can’t agree on what religion is, and Andrew Henry, creator of Religion for Breakfast, thinks that tells us something. In this conversation with Jonny Thomson, he explains why he looks at what religious practices do rather than what they claim, why a stadium chant and a church creed may be closer than they seem, and why “true Christianity” is harder to pin down than its defenders suggest. items.title: A modest proposal: Europe should go full bananas
items.description:
Underneath the political map of Europe’s nation-states simmers another reality: a tangle of economic and logistical corridors that transcend national borders. The best known of these is the Blue Banana.

items.title: We built our world on “Big Math.” Now we no longer understand it.
items.description:
Math has undeniably escaped the human mind and implanted itself in nearly every corner of the world. Over the past 75 years, as computers became commonplace and grew in power, what once amounted to mental arithmetic has become something else entirely. It’s not just math; it’s “Big Math,” too large for the human brain alone.
